tagline.text: A limestone cave at the foot of Bulacan's Sierra Madre where revolutionaries once hid

location.label: Location
location.text: Bigte area, Norzagaray, Bulacan, near Ipo Dam

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱150–400 (day trip round trip from Manila)

children.text: This limestone cave at the foot of the Sierra Madre in Norzagaray, north of Manila, is said to have served as a revolutionary base in 1896–1897. You borrow a helmet and flashlight and wade through a water-filled passage on a half-day caving trip.

Pinagrealan Cave is a limestone cave at the foot of the Sierra Madre in Norzagaray, Bulacan. It is often described as being near San Jose del Monte, but it administratively belongs to Norzagaray, and the usual approach passes through San Jose del Monte toward the Bigte rotunda. Some guides place it in Barangay Minuyan, so check the local signboard and a map app. It can be reached from central Manila by public transport in half a day, which has made it a well-known day-trip caving spot.
The cave is tied to Philippine revolutionary history. Pulling together blogs and the site signage, it was first known as the Minuyan Cave, and between

revolutionary forces under General Sinforoso del Cruz used it as a stronghold. Stories say the forces of Generals Emilio Aguinaldo and Pio del Pilar stayed here, and that a barracks and an infirmary for the wounded stood near the entrance. There are also accounts that the Japanese army used it as a refuge toward the end of World War II. These details rest on local signage and blog accounts, so they may differ from scholarly records.

Inside, the cave is dark and cool, with limestone features such as stalactites, stalagmites, columns and curtain-like calcite. Cold air flows out right at the entrance, and farther in a stream runs ankle-deep, rising to waist-deep in some sections. The total length is described as more than 1 km, but ordinary visitors only cover the section the guide leads, and the deep inner part is hard to enter without preparation because of the deep water.

The cave is a tourist site and also a conservation issue. Quarrying on the limestone mountain above it has raised concerns about blasting vibration and rockfall, and many posts say the nearby Lioness and Rhino rock formations were closed because of quarrying. A cave association and environmental groups have campaigned for its protection, so be sure to check whether the cave is currently open before you go. For first-timers, think of it as half historic site, half wet adventure. It is not a polished attraction and the facilities are simple, but seeing traces of the revolution and cave formations together, not far from Manila, is its appeal. If you bring children, consider their age and stamina because of the water depth and the darkness, and agree with the guide on how far to go.

Revolutionary forces are said to have stayed in this cave in 1896–1897. Signage and blogs describe a barracks and infirmary near the entrance and a residence for General Aguinaldo deeper inside. The guide tells the stories section by section.
You walk along an ankle-deep stream and, in some sections, wade through waist-deep water. Many visitors say the water feels cold at first but you soon get used to it. Expect to get wet.
Stalactites, stalagmites, columns, draperies and flowstone appear in the light of your headlamp. One source describes passages that are about 3–7 m high.

This is the section where General Aguinaldo's house is said to have stood behind rocks arranged like doors. Walking it while listening to the guide makes it easier to understand how the space was used.
Cold air comes out of the cave entrance even during the day. For travelers coming up from Manila in the hot season, it is a welcome way to cool off. You exit through the same entrance.

blocks.title: Helmet and flashlight rental and a place for bags

children.text: Some reviews say the entrance fee includes renting a helmet and flashlight. You can leave your bag at the station, and some posts mention a shower area, which eases the trip home in wet clothes. Check that the gear fits before you enter and tighten the helmet strap firmly.
The cave association says endemic and endangered bats, reptiles and birds live here. Avoid loud noises and do not touch the walls; observe quietly.

items.title: Day course from Manila
items.subtitle: Leave in the morning, return in the afternoon

children.text: Head from Quezon City to SM Fairview or an EDSA bus stop. Leaving early lets you return while there is still daylight.
Board a jeepney bound for Bigte at Fairview. According to reviews, it is a long ride of around an hour even without traffic.
Get off at the Bigte rotunda or Bigte market and take a tricycle or motorcycle taxi to the cave station. Pay the entrance fee there and receive a helmet and flashlight.
Enter with a guide. Allow about
1–1.5 hours
to walk the stream and hear the history, there and back.
Change clothes and rest at the station. If time allows, walk around the village or look around toward nearby Ipo Dam.
Take a jeepney back toward Fairview.
These times are an example based on reviews. Traffic and the station's operating hours change from day to day, so confirm locally.

Travel times vary greatly with traffic. Recheck the route on Google Maps before you leave.
From Norzagaray town proper, take a jeepney bound for Bigte and get off at the Bigte rotunda (traffic circle).
From the rotunda, hire a motorcycle taxi to the cave entrance. Some reviews mention walking about
Searching for "Pinagrealan Cave" in a map app gives the address 1562 Curvada Rd, Norzagaray. The last stretch is a narrow country road, so be careful with large vehicles.
Whether parking is available at the station has not been confirmed. Ask locally.
If public transport is inconvenient and your group is large, you can also rent a van in Manila and go straight to Bigte. Costs vary by operator and season, so get a quote.
During the dry season,
November–May
, the cave paths are relatively less slippery and getting around is easier. Because there is water inside, the cave actually feels cool in the midday heat.

In the rainy season, flooded country roads and rising water inside the cave are concerns. If a typhoon or heavy rain is forecast, it is safer not to enter, and you should ask the station whether the cave is open that day.

Weekends and holidays can draw crowds, so a weekday morning is more relaxed. However, a guide may not be on site on weekdays, so it helps to contact the station or the Bulacan provincial tourism office (PYSEACTO, phone +63 44 791 6604 listed in a review) before you visit. That number comes from a 2012 review, so there is no guarantee it still connects.

The area around the cave is a rural village with few places to stay and no large restaurants. Most visitors make a day trip from Manila or Quezon City, and those who stay overnight tend to look in Norzagaray town or toward San Jose del Monte.
For meals, use the small eateries and shops around Bigte market or the rotunda, and it is safer to bring water and snacks from Manila. A towel and a change of clothes are essential.

In short, the plan is to leave early in the morning and be ready to head back before lunch. Reviews say the last public transport from the Bigte area leaves early, so it is safer to leave the village by mid-afternoon at the latest. Assume the area near the station is the only place to rest after changing out of wet clothes, and bring plenty of water and snacks.
Bring your own flashlight or headlamp. Even if you can rent one, a spare light gives peace of mind.
Some sections are waist-deep, so wear clothes you do not mind getting wet and sandals or shoes that handle water.
Bring a change of clothes, a towel and a plastic bag for wet clothing. Reviews say the station has a shower area.
Leave your bag at the station if possible and take only your phone and a few essentials in a waterproof pouch.
The cave is entered and exited through the same entrance. A guide may suggest a narrow alternate route, but reviews say breathing is hard there, so do not push yourself.
Go with companions rather than alone, and always enter with a local guide.
Some reviews say the cave facilities are inside the Ipo Dam compound. Entry procedures may change, so check the notice at the entrance.
Rockfall risk from blasting at the quarry above the cave has been reported. Check whether the cave is open before you go, and do not enter after heavy rain.
A 2021 geological report and a cave association letter claim that quarry blasting shakes the cave. Check the current situation locally.
The deep inner sections have deep water and are dangerous without preparation. Go only as far as the guide allows.
Water levels rise when it rains. Do not enter if heavy rain or a typhoon is forecast.
Some posts say the Lioness and Rhino rocks have been closed or no longer exist because of quarrying. Do not approach without permission.
Entrance fees, guide fees and operating hours all come from reviews a few years old. Check the latest information.
